subthemes.text:
ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL

[6] In cases where a refugee protection claimant has citizenship in more than one country, as in the case at hand, he or she must establish the merits of the claim in respect of all of those countries.3 In this case, the appellants must demonstrate that they have a well-founded fear of being persecuted or of being subjected to the risks set out in subsection 97(1) of the IRPA, both in Italy and in Venezuela, in order to be granted refugee protection in Canada. Consequently, neither the RPD nor the RAD is required to review the fear of persecution or the availability of protection in the second country of citizenship once it has concluded that the appellants do not have a well-founded fear of persecution in the first country.5

[7] Consequently, although the RPD assessed the appellants' risk in Venezuela and in Italy and concluded that there was no risk for them in those two countries, my decision will focus solely on Italy.
Absence of a risk for the appellants in Italy

[8] The appellants argue in paragraph 26 of their appeal memorandum that despite the fact that the principal appellant failed to present any tangible evidence regarding the fear and the harm that she could suffer in Italy, one can understand that, given the reputation of the criminal groups that operate there, her statements could become reality.

[9] I am of the opinion that it is insufficient to cite the presence of criminal mafia groups in Italy to demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that the principal appellant and her children are facing a serious possibility of persecution or that they are subjected to a danger of torture, a risk to their lives or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in that country, where they have citizenship.

[10] The RPD questioned the principal appellant at the hearing and asked her to state what was preventing her from travelling to that country, where she and her children have citizenship, as can be seen from their Italian passports submitted into evidence.4 The principal appellant pointed out that she does not know anyone in Italy, that she has that citizenship from her father because he is Italian, that she has never been there, that there is corruption in that country, that her agent of harm also has Italian citizenship and had been extradited there, that he is imprisoned there, and that there are hitmen in that country. She testified that she did not consider the possibility of her and her children travelling to Italy because she would be alone there with three young children, without family, and would have to build her life there from scratch.

[11] It should be noted that the principal appellant's fear relating to Italy is quite vague. She acknowledged on appeal that she failed to present any tangible evidence pertaining to the fear and the harm that she and her children could face in Italy.5 Moreover, I do not see in the evidence on the record information demonstrating that the principal appellant and her children are currently at risk via hitmen or the Italian mafia.

[12] In these circumstances, I consider that the RPD did not err in its conclusion that it does not have any evidence establishing an actual risk, or even possible attempts to harm the principal appellant and her children in Italy. I am of the opinion that it is insufficient to simply cite on appeal the presence and the reputation of mafia groups in Italy.

[13] Consequently, I consider that the appellants failed to demonstrate that there is a serious possibility of persecution or a risk to their lives, or that they would be subjected to a danger of torture, a risk to their lives or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Italy.

subthemes.text:
[14] In light of the above, I am of the opinion that it was not necessary for the RPD to analyze state protection. Moreover, the appellants are not disputing the RPD's analysis in this regard. Nevertheless, I analyzed all of the evidence on this topic and, for the following reasons, I consider that the RPD did not err and that its decision is correct.

[15] The RPD considered the evidence submitted by the appellants, namely, an article dated XXXX XXXX, 2014, published on the XXXX XXXX website and reporting that a man named XXXX XXXX, a mafioso of Italian background from Venezuela, was extradited to Italy after being on the run for twenty years.6 The principal appellant stated that he was her friend. She testified that he was serving a twenty-year prison sentence there. In these circumstances, I consider, similar to the RPD, that the confirmation of the long-term imprisonment of the principal appellant's alleged agent of harm confirms that the Italian state and its institutions are functional.

[16] Furthermore, there is a well-established presumption that a state is able to protect its citizens. Except in situations of complete breakdown of the state apparatus, it should be assumed that the state is capable of protecting its citizens.7 In this case, Italy is a democracy and is not characterized by a complete breakdown of its state apparatus. As a result, we must presume that the Italian state is capable of protecting its citizens.

[17] In light of all of the above, there is nothing in the evidence on the record or in the principal appellant's claims that demonstrates that she and her children would not receive adequate protection in Italy should they need it. The onus is on her to establish, through clear and convincing evidence, that the Italian state cannot protect her and her children. However, she failed to rebut the presumption of Italian state protection. The RPD did not err.

[18] Considering all of the above, I conclude that the appellants failed to demonstrate a serious possibility that they would be persecuted or that they would be at risk of being subjected to a danger of torture, a risk to their lives, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Italy.

[7] Consequently, although the RPD assessed the appellants' risk in Venezuela and in Italy and concluded that there was no risk for them in those two countries, my decision will focus solely on Italy.
Absence of a risk for the appellants in Italy

[8] The appellants argue in paragraph 26 of their appeal memorandum that despite the fact that the principal appellant failed to present any tangible evidence regarding the fear and the harm that she could suffer in Italy, one can understand that, given the reputation of the criminal groups that operate there, her statements could become reality.

[9] I am of the opinion that it is insufficient to cite the presence of criminal mafia groups in Italy to demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that the principal appellant and her children are facing a serious possibility of persecution or that they are subjected to a danger of torture, a risk to their lives or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in that country, where they have citizenship.

[10] The RPD questioned the principal appellant at the hearing and asked her to state what was preventing her from travelling to that country, where she and her children have citizenship, as can be seen from their Italian passports submitted into evidence.4 The principal appellant pointed out that she does not know anyone in Italy, that she has that citizenship from her father because he is Italian, that she has never been there, that there is corruption in that country, that her agent of harm also has Italian citizenship and had been extradited there, that he is imprisoned there, and that there are hitmen in that country. She testified that she did not consider the possibility of her and her children travelling to Italy because she would be alone there with three young children, without family, and would have to build her life there from scratch.

[11] It should be noted that the principal appellant's fear relating to Italy is quite vague. She acknowledged on appeal that she failed to present any tangible evidence pertaining to the fear and the harm that she and her children could face in Italy.5 Moreover, I do not see in the evidence on the record information demonstrating that the principal appellant and her children are currently at risk via hitmen or the Italian mafia.

[12] In these circumstances, I consider that the RPD did not err in its conclusion that it does not have any evidence establishing an actual risk, or even possible attempts to harm the principal appellant and her children in Italy. I am of the opinion that it is insufficient to simply cite on appeal the presence and the reputation of mafia groups in Italy.

[13] Consequently, I consider that the appellants failed to demonstrate that there is a serious possibility of persecution or a risk to their lives, or that they would be subjected to a danger of torture, a risk to their lives or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Italy.

[14] In light of the above, I am of the opinion that it was not necessary for the RPD to analyze state protection. Moreover, the appellants are not disputing the RPD's analysis in this regard. Nevertheless, I analyzed all of the evidence on this topic and, for the following reasons, I consider that the RPD did not err and that its decision is correct.

[15] The RPD considered the evidence submitted by the appellants, namely, an article dated XXXX XXXX, 2014, published on the XXXX XXXX website and reporting that a man named XXXX XXXX, a mafioso of Italian background from Venezuela, was extradited to Italy after being on the run for twenty years.6 The principal appellant stated that he was her friend. She testified that he was serving a twenty-year prison sentence there. In these circumstances, I consider, similar to the RPD, that the confirmation of the long-term imprisonment of the principal appellant's alleged agent of harm confirms that the Italian state and its institutions are functional.

[16] Furthermore, there is a well-established presumption that a state is able to protect its citizens. Except in situations of complete breakdown of the state apparatus, it should be assumed that the state is capable of protecting its citizens.7 In this case, Italy is a democracy and is not characterized by a complete breakdown of its state apparatus. As a result, we must presume that the Italian state is capable of protecting its citizens.

[17] In light of all of the above, there is nothing in the evidence on the record or in the principal appellant's claims that demonstrates that she and her children would not receive adequate protection in Italy should they need it. The onus is on her to establish, through clear and convincing evidence, that the Italian state cannot protect her and her children. However, she failed to rebut the presumption of Italian state protection. The RPD did not err.

[18] Considering all of the above, I conclude that the appellants failed to demonstrate a serious possibility that they would be persecuted or that they would be at risk of being subjected to a danger of torture, a risk to their lives, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Italy.
CONCLUSION

[19] I dismiss the appeal and confirm the determination of the RPD that the appellants, XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXand XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
